articles.body: 256 contacts per list, 250 recipients to start on the API, and five messaging tiers. Here is how WhatsApp's limits work and how to design around them. If you are building customer notifications, reminders or campaigns on WhatsApp, the first thing that trips people up is the word "limit". There are two different systems with two different kinds of limit, and mixing them up leads to bad architecture decisions. Two systems, two kinds of limit WhatsApp Business App. This is the app a small business uses on a phone. Its traditional broadcast lists hold up to 256 contacts each. You can create many lists, but every recipient must have saved your number to receive the message. WhatsApp Business Platform (the API). This is the infrastructure you integrate with. There are no lists here.

articles.title: HEAD vs GET for link checking: HEAD is faster, and it lies more than you'd think
articles.excerpt: If you've ever written a link checker, you've had this thought: I don't need the page body, I just need the status code. I'll send HEAD. It's a reasonable instinct. HEAD is defined to return the same…
articles.body: If you've ever written a link checker, you've had this thought: I don't need the page body, I just need the status code. I'll send HEAD. It's a reasonable instinct. HEAD is defined to return the same headers as GET without the body, so it should be cheaper and give the same answer. In practice, a noticeable share of servers answer HEAD differently from GET, and a link checker that trusts HEAD ends up with false alarms, missed breakages, or both. Here's a direct comparison and the strategy I'd actually ship. The theory RFC 9110 says a server should send the same header fields for HEAD as it would for GET. Note the "should". Plenty of real-world stacks treat HEAD as an afterthought: Frameworks that route by method and never registered a HEAD handler.

articles.title: We shipped a period tracker without accounts, ads or analytics. The tradeoffs are real.
articles.excerpt: Monthly Rose went live on 7 October. No account system, no ad or analytics SDKs, no shop inside it. All the logging works offline, and if you turn on Apple Health it syncs both ways. That sounds like…
articles.body: Monthly Rose went live on 7 October. No account system, no ad or analytics SDKs, no shop inside it. All the logging works offline, and if you turn on Apple Health it syncs both ways. That sounds like a clean win. It isn't free. No accounts means no cross-device push campaign, no "you logged late this month" nudge, no funnel to stare at when the numbers dip. If someone's notifications go quiet, I find out when they email me — or don't. What's left is the unglamorous stuff. Cycle predictions are a most-likely day plus a range instead of one confident date, because irregular cycles exist and pretending otherwise is how you get people to distrust the whole app. Reminders say which rule fired, so turning one off is a decision instead of a shrug.

articles.title: Erasure Requests: Model Provider Cleanup From Reservations
articles.excerpt: When a product has to honor an erasure request, the cleanup obligation owed to a hosted model provider has to come from what was possibly sent, not from what we can prove was sent. We had it derived f…
articles.body: When a product has to honor an erasure request, the cleanup obligation owed to a hosted model provider has to come from what was possibly sent, not from what we can prove was sent. We had it derived from the wrong signal, and the two directions of that failure were not equally bad: one asks a vendor for a cleanup of data it never received, the other can leave personal data sitting at a vendor outside our control. What follows is the rule that replaced it, the SQL condition that implements it, a reversible migration (a database change you can roll back) that installs it, and a regression module that reproduces both defects. The product here is an onboarding system.

articles.body: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to create incentives for powerful AI models that make following the rules the most rational choice. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code.

articles.title: Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now
articles.excerpt: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight p…
articles.body: 6 Min Read Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now View of the Manned Spacecraft Center during construction in 1963. Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis. Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery. Johnson is home to America’s astronaut corps, the Mission Control Center, and the teams behind some of humanity’s greatest achievements in space.
